caption: Newanforbi v. HOPE et al.
claims: 42 U.S.C. § 1983: Procedural Due Process — Three Counts: (I) Damages against HOPE; (II) Injunctive/Declaratory Relief against HOPE & Macomber; (III) Delegation Without Safeguards against both
status: DISMISSED WITHOUT PREJUDICE — Notice of Voluntary Dismissal filed May 21, 2026; Minute Order entered June 1, 2026 (FRCP 41(a)(1)(A)(i); case closed; refiling preserved; ECF No. 5 Notice of Related Cases was not an answer or MSJ)
judge: Hon. Troy L. Nunley / Mag. Allison Claire
defendants: HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc. d/b/a HOPE PROGRAM (NPI 1992154603; for damages — Count I; injunctive/declaratory — Counts II–III); Jeff Macomber, Secretary CDCR (official capacity; injunctive/declaratory relief only — Counts II–III; Ex parte Young). [FAC narrowed from 9 original defendants — all individual CDCR defendants (Palacios, Bishop, Dodd, Moua, Noguchi, Derrick, Rojo) dropped in FAC filed Feb. 20, 2026.]
causes: Count I — 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Damages: Procedural Due Process (14th Amend.) — HOPE denied Plaintiff meaningful opportunity to be heard before discharge review; HOPE fabricated '10-year parole term' ineligibility rule; eight documented facial defects in Form 1502-DR; financial conflict of interest — HOPE billed CDCR ~$10,600/year per retained parolee (against HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc. for compensatory, nominal, and punitive damages)

Count II — 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Declaratory & Injunctive Relief (Ex parte Young): (a) HOPE's blanket retention policy violates procedural due process — judicially condemned in In re Dwyer (San Mateo Super. Ct. Mar. 20, 2023) and ACSOL v. Macomber (L.A. Super. Ct. Dec. 13, 2023); (b) CDCR's discharge review framework violates Cal. Penal Code §§ 3001(a)(2) and 3008(d)(2) and 15 CCR § 3574 (against HOPE and Macomber, official capacity)

Count III — 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Delegation Without Safeguards: CDCR delegated discharge authority to a financially conflicted private vendor (HOPE) without adequate procedural safeguards — HOPE's financial interest in retention creates structural bias that taints the entire discharge review framework (against HOPE and Macomber, official capacity)
key_facts: HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc. (Shannon Smith LCSW, owner; NPI 1992154603; 1245 B Street, Hayward CA 94541; ~$14.2M annual revenue; ~176 employees) operates under Master Contract No. 901949 ($1.65M → $2.2M pooled vendor contract through 2027) — a contract that pays HOPE ~$10,600/year per retained parolee, creating a structural financial conflict of interest in the discharge review process. HOPE charges: $75–$100/group session (90 min), $130–$200/individual session, $450–$600/polygraph, $1,000/psychosexual eval. CDCR delegates discharge recommendation authority to HOPE — a private for-profit entity with no state-law adjudicatory safeguards — under a scheme that West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42 (1988) makes actionable under §1983. HOPE's blanket retention policy (retain all participants regardless of progress) was judicially condemned in In re Dwyer (San Mateo Super. Ct. Mar. 20, 2023) and ACSOL v. Macomber (L.A. Super. Ct. Dec. 13, 2023). Eight documented facial defects in Form 1502-DR (the discharge review instrument): (1) no score, scale, or methodology disclosed; (2) 'High Risk' designation without actuarial basis; (3) 'Eagan' copy-paste error (wrong parolee's name); (4) unemployment cited as aggravating factor — caused by Defendants' own supervision conduct; (5) fabricated '10-year parole term' ineligibility rule with no statutory basis; (6) blanket retention recommendation regardless of individual progress; (7) no appeal mechanism disclosed; (8) HOPE financial interest in outcome undisclosed. Cal. Penal Code § 3001(a)(2) mandates discharge consideration at 5 years; § 3008(d)(2) limits retention criteria; 15 CCR § 3574 (effective Apr. 2025) mandates separation of treatment and discharge decisions — a structural mandate HOPE's phase-looping framework violates. HOPE is a for-profit LCSW corporation with no qualified immunity. Original complaint (Doc 1, Jan. 22, 2026) named 9 defendants including individual CDCR officers; FAC (Doc 4, Feb. 20, 2026) strategically narrowed to HOPE (damages) and Macomber (injunctive/declaratory) to focus attack on structural defects and avoid qualified immunity defenses. HOPE appeared through SLB (Cynthia G. Lawrence SBN 148927 / Blaze Van Dine SBN 251946, Sims Lawrence & Broghammer) via Notice of Related Cases (ECF No. 5, May 20, 2026) — identifying related cases: Matter 3 (Derrick, 2:26-cv-0004) and this matter — the first and only paper served by any defendant. Voluntary Dismissal Without Prejudice filed May 21, 2026 — one day after HOPE's first appearance — under FRCP 41(a)(1)(A)(i): no defendant had served an answer or MSJ; the Notice of Related Cases is neither. Dismissal is self-executing, without prejudice, not an adjudication on the merits per FRCP 41(a)(1)(B). Each party bears own costs/fees. Refiling preserved.
procedural_status: Complaint filed Jan. 22, 2026; FAC Feb. 20, 2026 narrowed to HOPE and Macomber. HOPE appeared May 20 via Notice of Related Cases (ECF No. 5). Notice of Voluntary Dismissal Without Prejudice filed May 21 under FRCP 41(a)(1)(A)(i); Minute Order June 1 closed the case without prejudice — refiling preserved. SLB's May 23 settlement letter still addressed this action as pending. Dated docket beats live in timeline.json.
damages: FAC: Economic damages >$100,000 lost CDL earnings against HOPE (Macomber caused CDL suspension through HOPE's discharge-blocking scheme); punitive damages against HOPE (financial conflict of interest, deliberate indifference to constitutional rights); nominal damages $1; injunctive and declaratory relief against both defendants; costs and attorneys' fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988.
risk: HOPE has NO qualified immunity (private entity — Owen v. City of Independence, 445 U.S. 622 (1980)). West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42 (1988) — HOPE exercises a function traditionally and exclusively reserved to the state (parole discharge recommendation); delegated function theory strong. Financial conflict of interest (§10,600/year per retained parolee) supports deliberate indifference and punitive damages. Blanket retention policy already twice judicially condemned. Voluntary dismissal without prejudice preserves full refiling rights — case can be refiled in federal or state court.
